articles.title: Amid AI Hype, Autodesk Turns the Spotlight on Human Makers
articles.fullContent:
By Richard Lowe The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

As AI reshapes what’s possible, Autodesk wants to inspire people to create what matters.

The technology company, which makes design software for industries including architecture, manufacturing, and media, has launched its latest campaign, “The World Is Yours for the Making,” created by Giant Spoon.

A new spot, directed by Salomon Ligthelm, takes a humanistic tone, opening on a newborn swaddled in a hospital blanket. A narrator says, “Consider this a user manual for planet Earth. A simple guide that begins like this: Make something.”

What follows is a montage of humans using their creativity to shape the world: An architect designs a sports arena, then later attends a soccer game there; a father creates an animated version of his daughter’s teddy bear.

The final line of narration is a call to action: “Make what matters.”

According to Dara Treseder , CMO at Autodesk, the campaign makes clear that the company sees technology, and AI, as a tool for people. It’s launching at a moment when 39% of Americans believe AI does more harm than good, according to the latest Bentley University-Gallup Business in Society research .

“There are two questions every technology company has to answer at this moment. The first one is, ‘Who is technology for?’ And the second one is, ‘As the technology gets more powerful, what do we want to compound?’” Treseder told ADWEEK. “Technology is for people. What we want to compound is human ingenuity, human agency, and ultimately human progress for good and for everyone.”

The spot debuts today (Sept. 9) and will run on linear TV in New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles during the NFL Kickoff Game between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. It will also air across Autodesk-owned channels, CTV, and social.

Treseder has led Autodesk’s marketing team since 2022, overseeing campaigns with a range of styles and tones. “Let There Be Anything” took a comedic approach , showing how Autodesk products help people create things that even God (Tony Hale) finds impressive. “Otto Desc,” an ad highlighting Autodesk’s presence in Hollywood, aired during the 2023 Academy Awards, styled as a parody of a tribute documentary .

Now, as AI stirs anxiety and uncertainty, especially among Gen Z , Treseder said a more emotional angle was necessary to meet the moment.

“We’re surrounded by AI hype. We’re surrounded by big questions about what technology means for people,” Treseder said. “We wanted to make sure that our customers understand that we are their trusted partner as they navigate these things. This was not the right moment for humor.”

There’s more to come. Over the next 12 months, “The World Is Yours for the Making” will serve as Autodesk’s platform for human-focused, emotional stories about the people who design and make things.

“It’s so important to us that we meet our customers where they are emotionally,” Treseder said.

Treseder and her team take pride in knowing Autodesk’s customers on an intimate level. Beyond product surveys and focus groups, she spends a lot of time interacting with them personally.

“I like a good conversation,” Treseder said. “I go to their shops. I go to their businesses. I immerse myself with them all around the world. There are some things you can only get by immersing yourself.”

Several of the people featured in “The World Is Yours for the Making” are Autodesk’s real customers, a decision that kept the focus on the people who use the company’s tools.

“Our mission is to empower everyone everywhere to design and make anything. We’re helping, but our customers are the ones designing and making all of these incredible things in the world. What better way to center on them than to ensure that the cast is reflective of our real customers,” Treseder said.

From Aerie to Equinox, Brands Are Leaning Into AI Fears Richard Lowe

Richard Lowe is a freelance writer based in Los Angeles.

articles.title: New Hyundai Campaign Casts Childhood Cancer Survivors As Warriors
articles.fullContent:
ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ brings the people shaping advertising, commerce, and media together for four days of unscripted conversations and after-hours connections. Meet us in Midtown, Oct. 5–8.

For nearly three decades, Hyundai has used a colorful handprint as the calling card for its initiative to support pediatric cancer patients and their families. This year, the automaker is giving its long-running Hope on Wheels campaign a fierce makeover.

Hyundai Hope on Wheels, the brand’s 28-year-old program supporting childhood cancer research and patients, is launching a new campaign this September for Pediatric Cancer Awareness Month. But unlike a typical automotive campaign, there isn’t a Hyundai vehicle in the hero spot.

Instead, the ad opens with a small child dressed as a gladiator, representing the warrior spirit of kids facing cancer and the network of support that surrounds them. Called “Little Warrior,” the spot is meant to celebrate the strength and resilience of these young patients, while reinforcing Hyundai Hope on Wheels’ mission to help end childhood cancer.

The campaign grew out of conversations with Hyundai Hope on Wheels’ child ambassadors, Hyundai CEO Sean Gilpin told Adweek. These ambassadors, who are survivors of childhood cancer turned advocates, expressed that they wanted to give other patients the same sense of confidence and determination they had found during treatment.

“They said, there were days where we’re scared, or there were days that we weren’t feeling great, but we never gave up this fighting spirit,” Gilpin told Adweek, speaking on behalf of the child ambassadors.

That insight led the team to the idea of warriors using paint and symbols before heading into battle, Gilpin said. The familiar Hope on Wheels handprint became a visual shorthand for that idea, although this campaign represents a shift in the campaign scope and purpose.

As a part of the Hope on Wheels revamp, Hyundai has also created a series of “warrior gowns” that pediatric cancer patients can wear during treatment. The design of the gowns, which are depicted in the ad spot, were inspired by a mom who created princess pajamas to replace her daughter’s itchy hospital gown, earning her the nickname “princess warrior,” Gilpin told Adweek.

Hyundai has donated 2,000 gowns to children’s hospitals in Southern California and plans to distribute additional gowns nationwide, Gilpin said, with its dealers matching the donations. The company is also distributing handprint decals to Hyundai owners and new-vehicle buyers, giving them a physical way to signal their support and raise awareness of the campaign.

The campaign is also stretching beyond conventional paid media, with partners including NBC and Amazon expanding Hyundai’s reach. NBC will air the Hope on Wheels ad during Sunday night football broadcasts, while Amazon is supporting the effort through a “Stream It Forward” program that Hyundai says will generate approximately $500,000 in additional contributions based on views during the campaign period.

“We don’t necessarily have to make this about Hope on Wheels,” Gilpin said of conversations with media partners. “We just want this about pediatric cancer.”

Even the Jonas Brothers have joined the effort, partnering with Hyundai on their podcast and recently visiting a fan in a children’s hospital.

That approach marks a notable evolution for a program that Hyundai has supported for 28 years. The company has long used the initiative to fund research and support patients, but Gilpin said it has historically stopped short of making Hope on Wheels a major marketing platform. The “Little Warrior” campaign changes that while deliberately keeping the brand in the background.

“There’s not a car in this commercial because this commercial is not about our product,” Gilpin said. “It’s just our mission as a brand.”

articles.title: Brand safety in 2026: Enterprise policy framework
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Brand safety is the practice of protecting a brand’s reputation by controlling where and how it appears online, from ad placements to social media publishing.
  2. The most common brand safety risks in 2026 include AI-generated misinformation, ad adjacency to harmful content, bot amplification, and unvetted influencer partnerships.
  3. Internal brand safety policies give enterprise teams clear roles, approval workflows, content standards, and escalation plans so nothing gets published without the right checks.
  4. Tools like Hootsuite Social OS help enforce brand safety at scale through governed workflows, real-time listening, and AI-powered content review.

What is brand safety?

Brand safety is the set of practices that keep a brand’s ads, content, and conversations away from harmful, offensive, or misleading environments. It applies to paid media, where an ad might appear next to violent or extremist content, and to organic social, where a poorly reviewed post or an unmoderated comment thread can create the same reputational damage.

Most enterprise teams anchor their approach to industry standards. The Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), a voluntary cross-industry initiative created in 2019 that the World Federation of Advertisers discontinued on August 9, 2024, produced the Brand Safety Floor, which defined the content categories advertisers universally avoid, such as hate speech, explicit content, and terrorism.

Although the initiative itself no longer operates, its Brand Safety Floor and Adjacency Standards Framework remain widely used as legacy industry reference points. The IAB and accredited verification vendors then measure whether placements actually stayed inside those lines.

The practical point for marketers: Brand safety is not a single tool or a one-time audit. It is a system of standards, workflows, and monitoring that has to work across every team touching your brand. For a broader look at the fundamentals, see our guide to protecting your brand across social channels.

Brand safety vs. brand suitability

Brand safety is about avoiding content that no advertiser wants to be near, while brand suitability is about deciding what’s appropriate for your specific brand, audience, and moment. Safety is the universal floor. Suitability is where your own values, category, and risk tolerance come in.

A news article about a natural disaster clears the brand safety floor. It may still be unsuitable for a travel brand running a beach campaign. Both decisions matter, but they’re made by different people using different criteria.

In short: Safety keeps you out of trouble, suitability keeps you on-brand.

What are the most common brand safety risks in 2026?

The risk landscape has shifted as AI-generated content, automated amplification, and creator-led media have all scaled at once. Most incidents enterprise teams face today fall into one of five categories.

  • Ad placement next to harmful or inappropriate content
  • Bots, trolls, and coordinated inauthentic behavior
  • Unvetted influencer partnerships
  • Misinformation and AI-generated deepfakes
  • Hashtag and trend hijacking

Ad placement next to harmful or inappropriate content

Programmatic buying accounts for over 90% of US digital display ad spending, which means adjacency decisions happen faster than any human can review them. A single misconfigured campaign can put your logo next to content that contradicts everything your brand stands for.

Inclusion lists (approved placements only) give tighter control than exclusion lists, which chase problems after they appear. Most enterprise teams run both, paired with keyword and category blocks, and audit placement reports monthly rather than at campaign wrap.

Bots, trolls, and coordinated inauthentic behavior

Automated accounts can flood a comment section, distort sentiment data, and make a minor complaint look like a mass backlash. Coordinated groups do the same thing deliberately, often targeting brands during product launches or public announcements.

The danger is not just the noise. It’s that teams overreact to manufactured outrage or miss a genuine issue buried underneath it. Reliable listening data and a clear threshold for what counts as a real incident help teams tell the difference.

Unvetted influencer partnerships

When a creator’s past content or ongoing behavior surfaces mid-campaign, the association lands on your brand. Vetting has to cover more than follower counts: past posts, audience authenticity, brand conflicts, and how the creator handles criticism.

articles.title: Samsung U.S. Marketing Chief Allison Stransky to Join Boston Beer Co. as CMO
articles.fullContent:
By Ryan Joe The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Samsung U.S. CMO Allison Stransky will become CMO of The Boston Beer Co. on Oct. 12, reporting to Boston Beer Company cofounder and chief executive officer Jim Koch and company chief operating officer Phil Hodges.

Boston Beer Company is known for ciders and beers including Truly Hard Seltzer, Samuel Adams, Twisted Tea, and the non-alcoholic beer General Admission—a variety that reflects Boston Beer’s active pursuit of American consumers’ shifting drinking habits .

But Stransky will have her work cut out for her. Two of the company’s top brands—Twisted Tea and the hard seltzer Truly—are struggling right now.

Twisted Tea dominates the niche of malt-based hard tea, but it’s facing stiff competition from spirits-based hard teas and canned cocktails, according to the company’s earnings call in July.

Meanwhile, consumer demand for Truly hasn’t met Boston Beer’s expectations, according to Koch on that same earnings call.

Boston Beer will still spend heavily on ads, but it’s cutting about $20 million in media that doesn’t perform as well, primarily for Truly.

In a statement , Stransky hailed Boston Beer’s vast portfolio. “I’ve long admired its ability to blend creativity, innovation, and storytelling to connect with consumers, and I’m excited to join this talented team and help build on the company’s strong foundation and drive future growth,” she said.

In her three years at Samsung U.S., Stransky also had an expansive mandate, overseeing marketing campaigns for the electronics giant’s huge roster of mobile devices, home appliances, and services to connect them all .

She is joining a company that hasn’t had a permanent CMO since March, after Boston Beer’s longtime marketing chief Lesya Lysyj stepped down . During that gap, Hodges served as interim CMO.

“Allison brings a fresh perspective shaped by experience at some of the world’s leading companies, along with a genuine passion for brand building and innovation, and we look forward to welcoming her to Boston Beer,” Koch said in a statement.

Boston Beer Company declined to comment beyond its statement.

Samsung did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

Ryan Joe is the editor in chief of Adweek.

What is a social intelligence tool?

A social intelligence tool helps brands turn online conversations into insights about their audience, market, and broader culture.

These tools mostly deal with unprompted data. People aren’t filling out a survey. They’re venting, joking, sharing recommendations in forums, and filming reviews for YouTube and TikTok.

That gives marketers access to millions of spontaneous mini focus groups happening all across social.

Bonus !!!

Discover the best way to gather insights and intel from your audience, competitors, industry, and favorite aspirational brands in our complete guide to advanced social listening .

Download now

Social intelligence vs. social listening vs. social media analytics

All three run on social data, but they answer different questions:

  • Social media analytics is about performance: How is our social content performing?
  • Social listening is about conversation: What are people saying about our brand, competitors, or industry?
  • Social intelligence pushes more into interpretation: What do those conversations actually tell us about our audience, our market, and what we should do next?

Here’s a quick breakdown of the biggest differences:

So, when should you take the leap to social intelligence?

Dylan Peterkin, a social intelligence expert, says teams tend to outgrow basic listening tools when their goals “move past performance and shift into understanding audiences and culture.”

A basic tool can help you measure what you spent on an idea and how it performed with your existing audience, but there’s no replacement for full-fledged intelligence: being where your target audience is, and finding ways to exist in those spaces naturally through product AND content.

In short, once your questions get bigger than campaign performance, basic listening starts to feel pretty limited.

What should you look for in a social intelligence tool?

Look for broad data coverage, real noise reduction, trend and theme detection, and AI-powered analysis, all wrapped in an interface your whole team can actually understand. 

Let’s take a closer look at what to look out for:

Data coverage

Before you can monitor conversations, you need to make sure you’re in the right rooms.

Say an intelligence tool covers the big social platforms but misses the Reddit rabbit holes and niche forums where your audience hangs out. You’re only working with a partial picture.

That’s why Peterkin starts with data coverage. “I need to understand where the gaps are, both for my own goals as an org and for the reputation of the company at the forefront,” he says.

The right coverage can also extend beyond social media. For example, Peterkin points to online reviews as another valuable source.

“Review site tracking alongside social data is a powerful storytelling combination that not every tool offers,” he shares. “Every brand should be using both alongside customer support data to understand the customer journey and uncover real pain points and whitespace opportunities, both on and off social media.”

Noise reduction

Social media is never short on opinions. The problem is that not all opinions tell you something useful.

By Robert Klara The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Veteran marketer Emma Chalwin, who’s done multi-year runs at Adobe Systems and Salesforce, will join Accenture as its new CMO, the company announced today.

Chalwin has most recently served as CMO at Workday, where she oversaw global marketing for the SaaS giant and focused on what she has termed “AI as a catalyst for success.” Prior to that post, Chalwin rose through the marketing ranks at Salesforce, going from marketing leader in the London office to San Francisco, where she ended her run as EVP of global field marketing.

articles.title: Social media archiving in 2026: A compliance guide
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media archiving captures posts, comments, edits, deletions, and metadata in a legally defensible format for regulatory compliance.
  2. Government, finance, healthcare, and education sectors face distinct archiving mandates under FOIA, SEC/FINRA, HIPAA, and FERPA.
  3. Compliant workflows require automated real-time capture, metadata preservation, searchable storage, and regular audits.
  4. Enterprise platforms like Hootsuite Social OS integrate with archiving solutions to automate compliance across teams and accounts.

What is social media archiving?

Social media archiving is the process of capturing, preserving, and storing all social media content in a secure, legally defensible format. That includes posts, comments, direct messages, multimedia, edits, deletions, and the metadata behind all of it.

Social media posted by government agencies is generally treated as a public record under FOIA and state open records laws, and in finance and healthcare, social messages count as regulated business communications.

For government agencies, social media is a public forum and must be archived as part of open records laws. Financial institutions, healthcare providers, and educational institutions face their own archiving mandates under regulations like SEC/FINRA rules, HIPAA, and FERPA.

A proper archive of your social media content and communication allows you to respond to eDiscovery, public records, and Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. You also need archived social comments if you are faced with a First Amendment challenge.

Your content is publicly available on your social accounts, but that’s not enough. Social media platforms are private-sector companies. They are not subject to open records laws, and there’s no guarantee they will preserve your content indefinitely.

Platform API changes can also restrict access to historical data without warning. A purpose-built archiving solution is the only way to maintain a complete, tamper-proof record.

Bonus: Download a free bundle of social media tools designed specifically for government — including post ideas and templates for social media policies, strategies, reports, and crisis communications.

Why is social media archiving important for regulated industries?

Social media archiving is a foundational risk management strategy that protects regulated organizations from legal exposure while building public trust. Without a systematic archiving process, agencies and institutions risk being unable to respond to records requests, audits, or litigation.

  • Legal compliance: Federal, state, and industry-specific regulations require organizations to retain social media records for defined periods. Archiving ensures you meet those obligations.
  • Audit readiness: Regulators can request records at any time. A searchable, well-organized archive means your team can respond quickly and completely.
  • eDiscovery preparedness: In legal proceedings, social media content is increasingly subject to discovery requests. Archived records with metadata provide the documentation courts require.
  • Risk mitigation: Archiving protects your organization from penalties, fines, and lawsuits that result from incomplete or missing records.
  • Transparency and public trust: For government agencies especially, accessible archives demonstrate accountability to constituents and the media.
  • Operational efficiency: Centralized, searchable archives reduce the time and effort required to locate specific content across multiple accounts and platforms.

Social media compliance starts with having the records to prove it.

How is social media archiving regulated across industries?

Regulations differ by state, country, and industry, but the core obligation is the same: preserve everything. Social media content is generally treated as part of the public record or as a business communication, subject to specific retention and privacy requirements.

Regulated organizations need to maintain an archive of social media content, including posts, comments, direct messages, and conversations. These records must be accessible for audits, public information requests, and legal discovery.

While the specific requirements differ by sector, most regulations require the following:

  • Metadata collection: Capturing timestamps, user information, and device details for every post and comment.
  • Original format retention: Preserving content exactly as it appeared when published, including edits and deletions.
  • Retention period: Storing records for a legally defined period, which varies by jurisdiction and industry.
  • Comment archiving: Retaining comments, even if they are edited, deleted, or hidden.
  • Contextual recordkeeping: Maintaining entire conversation threads, not just isolated comments.
  • Data location: Storing data in specific geographic regions to comply with privacy laws.

By Matt Britton The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Financial health remains one of the most significant influences on personal wellbeing, yet many people enter adulthood without the tools to manage it effectively.

As technology advances, the gap between having financial data and taking meaningful action is finally closing through intelligent platforms. The future of consumer finance is headed towards a blend of sophisticated automation and trusted human expertise.

In this episode of The Speed of Culture podcast, Mark Notarainni, EVP and general manager of Intuit’s Consumer Group, joins Matt Britton to share how Intuit is empowering millions to take control of their financial lives.

They discuss how consumer finance through platforms like TurboTax and Credit Karma have evolved over the years.

The conversation covers how AI helps people manage debt, the power of human expertise in digital tools, and why financial literacy is hitting younger generations differently.

Mark Notarainni is the EVP and general manager of Intuit’s Consumer Group, where he leads the strategy for a massive consumer ecosystem designed to help people save money, pay off debt, and improve their financial health. His leadership oversees iconic brands like TurboTax, which provides millions of people with tools for DIY, assisted, and full-service tax preparation, and Credit Karma, which helps people do everything from build credit, pay down debt and maximize their credit card rewards.

Mark previously served as Intuit’s chief customer success officer, where he was instrumental in launching the Virtual Expert Platform, connecting consumers with human expertise to drive more confident decisions. With a career at Intuit spanning over 15 years, he has a long history of creating technology-driven experiences rooted in empathy.

[08:43] Solving Kitchen Table Finances — Mark explains the concept of “kitchen table finances,” referring to the real-time decisions families make to manage their lives, such as balancing checkbooks or paying bills. He highlights how digital tools now allow people to handle these manual tasks instantly, helping them get ahead and make better decisions every single day.

[11:58] The Proactive Sentinel: AI in Finance — Mark shares how agents now monitor revolving debt, comparing a user’s situation against a marketplace of lenders to potentially save them hundreds of dollars a month automatically. This removes the traditional hurdles of financial management by doing the heavy lifting for the consumer.

[14:55] The Largest Paycheck of the Year — For many Americans, a tax refund is the biggest single payment they receive, averaging around $3,500. Mark describes how Intuit uses this moment to help users go from short-term survival to long-term health by making it easy to put that money into high-yield savings or pay down debt.

[15:35] AI Plus Human Intelligence (HI) — Mark details the “AI plus HI” philosophy, where technology handles data entry while humans provide the confident advice needed for big life decisions. He notes that the role of experts like CPAs is changing from manual labor to high-value advising, which inspires confidence in consumers. A combination that ensures that users have both the speed of technology and the empathy of a human professional when it matters most.

[24:36] The Power of Perseverance — When reflecting on his career journey, Mark identifies perseverance as his most significant driver and a core value he has passed down to his children. He believes that because change is constant, the ability to embrace new technology and stay ambitious is more important than ever. Success in the modern workforce comes from taking agency over your career and looking for ways to use new tools to your advantage.

Matt Britton is America’s leading expert on the millennial generation having consulted for over half of the Fortune 500 over the past two decades. He is the Founder and CEO of Suzy and the host of The Speed of Culture Podcast.

articles.fullContent:
By Jenny Rooney The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Some of the biggest opportunities for marketing leaders exist in industries where marketing has historically had the least influence.

In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, host Jenny Rooney sits down with Danielle Wuschke Paige, chief marketing and growth officer at Nixon Peabody, to explore what it takes to modernize marketing in a complex, relationship-driven industry.

Danielle shares how her B2B and agency background prepared her for legal marketing, and why trust and content matter more than flashy creative.

She also explains how she’s evolving the marketing function through stronger business strategy, thought leadership, and AI adoption.

Why strong B2B marketing fundamentals can transfer across industries, even when the category itself is completely unfamiliar

How to turn marketing into a more strategic business function by helping stakeholders understand its impact on firm performance, reputation, and growth

Why legal marketing is content-first and how timely expertise can build trust with clients who want more guidance from their advisors

How to balance a law firm’s overall brand with the individual reputations of attorneys whose personal credibility often drives business

Why AI should enhance junior marketers rather than replace the foundational skills of writing, creative thinking, and communication

Danielle Wuschke Paige is the chief marketing and growth officer at Nixon Peabody, an Am Law 100 firm with offices across the United States and internationally. She leads the firm’s marketing and business development organization, with responsibility spanning brand strategy, communications, client engagement, strategic pursuits, digital, design, industry marketing, and practice growth.

Danielle began her career in technology sales before moving into strategic marketing and then spending more than 15 years in the agency world, including leadership roles at FleishmanHillard and MSL.

[7:10] Modernizing An Old-School Marketing Function — Danielle explains that legal marketing historically lagged behind other industries, with teams focused heavily on executional tasks rather than strategic brand building. At Nixon Peabody, the opportunity was to rethink that model entirely by connecting marketing activity to firm-wide growth, practice priorities, industry focus, and individual attorney development. The shift required more than a visual refresh. It meant helping lawyers understand why stronger brand management, more sophisticated marketing, and a broader channel strategy could directly support the business.

[13:20] Why Legal Marketing Starts With Trust — Marketing a full-service law firm means supporting very different practices, industries, and individual attorneys while still presenting one consistent firm brand. Danielle says trust sits at the center of that challenge. Nixon Peabody’s 2024 client engagement survey revealed that clients wanted to hear from the firm three times more often than they actually did, particularly through timely, useful content that helped them understand fast-moving legal and business issues. That insight reinforces why legal marketing is fundamentally content-first and why relevance and credibility matter more than volume.

[21:06] Individual Attorneys Can Be The Strongest Brand Asset — Danielle explains that while the law firm brand carries important equity, the reputation of an individual attorney can be an even stronger driver of business. Well-known partners bring credibility into specific industries and practices, and that reputation creates a ripple effect across their wider teams. As a result, a major part of legal marketing is partner-first reputation building: helping attorneys develop visible expertise and thought leadership that strengthens both their own profile and the firm around them.

[27:44] AI Will Change Legal Work, But Not Replace Legal Expertise — Danielle describes AI as both a major opportunity and a technology that legal firms must approach with unusual care. Nixon Peabody is already using AI internally for workflow, analysis, firm data, and marketing experimentation, but the human layer remains essential. She argues that AI can help teams move faster and broaden how they think, yet junior professionals still need core skills in writing, communication, and creative judgment. The same applies to legal work itself: AI may reshape how services are delivered, but experienced attorneys will still be needed to provide the judgment and perspective clients rely on.

By Mark Mwachiro Friday will mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, and the various news networks are covering the solemn anniversary with special programming from the three locations directly impacted on that catastrophic day, including New York City, Washington, D.C., and Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

Here is how each network will cover the morning events honoring those lost and the heroes from that fateful day, which changed America and the world’s trajectory. ( All times Eastern .)

At 6 a.m., C-SPAN’s Washington Journal will be live with viewer calls and archival material from September 11, 2001.

The network will air live events from the 9/11 Memorial in New York City, the Pentagon, and the National Flight 93 Memorial in Pennsylvania.

If you’re creating good content but it’s not getting the love it deserves, you may have a distribution problem. 

Luckily, you’re in the right place. We’ll break down how to build a content distribution strategy, choose the right channels, and get more mileage out of every asset.

Key takeaways

  1. A content distribution strategy gives your content somewhere to go. It maps out where your content shows up and how it looks.
  2. Owned, earned, and paid channels all play different roles. Most brands use all three, but the balance looks different for everyone.
  3. Great content doesn’t distribute itself. A good repurposing workflow can turn one strong asset into weeks of content.
  4. Perch by Hootsuite keeps distribution from getting messy. Plan, schedule, and manage content across multiple channels from one place.

What is a content distribution strategy?

A content distribution strategy is a plan for getting your content in front of the right audience, using a mix of owned, earned, and paid channels.

A social-first approach takes it a step further by repurposing content for different social channels — like a 30-second clip for TikTok or a thread for X. Same content, but packaged in a way that feels native to each platform.

Do it better with Hootsuite, the all-in-one social media tool. Stay on top of things, grow, and beat the competition.

Owned vs. earned vs. paid distribution

Content distribution generally falls into three buckets: owned, earned, and paid. What separates them is who controls the channel and whether you’re paying for the placement.

Most brands benefit from a combo of all three, but that doesn’t mean you should invest in them equally.

Owned channels give you a foundation you actually control. Earned distribution lends you credibility. And paid distribution is how you put your best content in front of a specific audience, at whatever scale you can afford.

Why do you need a content distribution strategy?

A content distribution strategy helps your best work travel further. It gives you a plan to reach more people, extend the life of high-value assets, and shape each piece for the channels where it has the best chance to land.

Great content doesn’t automatically get reach

You can pour your heart into creating a great piece of content, but that doesn’t guarantee people will see it.

Facebook, for example, has an average engagement rate of only 0.15%. Over on Instagram, it isn’t much better at 0.48%. So if your last post underperformed, that’s not bad luck. It’s just the reality of organic reach in 2026.

Source: Statista

A distribution strategy is what actually changes those odds. It gives you a plan to reshare and repackage your content for other channels, giving it more than one shot at finding an audience.

It extends the lifespan of high-value assets

A solid distribution strategy puts your best content to work for longer. It turns one webinar into a handful of short clips. A blog post into a carousel. A research report into weeks of LinkedIn posts from your CEO.

That also takes some pressure off your content calendar. Instead of creating new content for every platform, you’re finding fresh angles in work you’ve already done.

It meets your audience where they are

Your audience isn’t hanging out in one place, and they’re definitely not consuming content in the same way.

articles.title: Real Estate Marketing: A Complete Guide for 2026
articles.fullContent:
If you’re running marketing for a real estate brand, you already know the deal. Zillow, Realtor.com, and Redfin sit at the top of nearly every high-volume query, and AI Overviews are quietly compressing what’s left of the informational clicks below. That’s the real estate marketing challenge in 2026. Everyone else has already adopted the basics, so pulling ahead now takes a creative, targeted strategy.

This guide walks through a five-step framework for building a real estate marketing plan. From there, you’ll get a breakdown of how AI search and portal competition are reshaping the search engine results pages (SERPs), plus a client case study showing what real growth looks like when the strategy lands.

You’ll finish this guide with a clear picture of what to do next for your real estate marketing strategy in 2026.

Key Takeaways

  • Zillow, Realtor.com, and Redfin dominate head-term SERPs, so marketing wins come from targeting long-tail and hyperlocal queries the portals ignore. 
  • Google’s AI Overviews are causing people to click less. Structure content for AI citation and reinforce E-E-A-T signals to stay visible. 
  • A five-step marketing plan (ICPs, brand identity, website, omnichannel, offline) is the foundation. Skip a step and everything downstream weakens. 
  • Owned channels like email and direct mail are how “the little guy” can fight against the real estate giants by routing buyers around third-party portals. 
  • NP Digital used the tactics in this guide to stack significant wins for our client, Homeway Real Estate.

What Is Real Estate Marketing?

Real estate marketing is the practice of promoting properties available for sale or rent. It takes the Four Ps of marketing (Product, Price, Place, and Promotion) and adapts them to the real estate market. 

The marketing plan is important because of the hyper-competitive nature of the real estate industry. A proper strategy could give you a powerful competitive edge. 

Here are the three main benefits of marketing for real estate professionals: 

  • Builds trust with the customer base: A consistent presence assures potential buyers that they’re dealing with the right person to help them find their dream property. 
  • Makes the brand more memorable: A recognizable brand increases the chances that buyers will seek the brand out when they enter the market. 
  • Enables more efficient selling: A long-term marketing strategy provides established channels to quickly promote new properties when they become available, cutting down on promotion and admin costs. 

National Association of Realtors (NAR) data tells us that every buyer uses the internet at some point during their home search, and 46 percent take their first step online (versus 20 percent who start by contacting an agent). The marketing strategy used could be the difference between a brokerage that compounds visibility for years and one that keeps starting from zero on every new listing.

How to Build a Real Estate Marketing Plan

You can develop a solid real estate marketing management plan in five simple steps. The order matters because each step sets up the next, so don’t skip anything. It usually means going back to fix something later.

We’ll start with the most important step of any marketing plan: defining who you’re trying to reach. From there, we’ll discuss your brand’s presence and finish with the optimal digital strategy, as well as offline channels you can use to supplement it. 

Here’s how the framework breaks down.

1. Define Your Ideal Customer Profiles (ICPs)

What type of people would make ideal sellers or renters?

Even if you understand your ideal customer, it’s important to map them out clearly on paper. These definitions will form the basis of the real estate marketing plan you implement, so ICPs could always use more fine-tuning. The more detailed, the better.

Most agents typically target several distinct ICPs that cover a whole portfolio of properties. 

Here are three example ICPs: 

  • Three to four-person families with a joint annual income of $150,000 looking to purchase suburban detached or semi-detached houses.
  • Young professionals with high disposable income searching for inner-city apartments to rent in the $2000 to $3000/month price range with an active local nightlife nearby.
  • Retirees with a budget of $300,000 to $500,000 in the market for semi-rural properties with good car access to local amenities like hospitals, supermarkets, and shops.

Research the following attributes when putting together your customer profiles:

  • Budget for rent or purchase
  • Desired location and property type
  • Specific property features (garage, bathrooms, garden)
  • Timeline (weeks or months)
  • Required nearby amenities (schools, transport, roads, etc.)

Treat these definitions as segmentation blocks you can plan against. Each ICP needs its own creative and channel mix. It also makes sense to give each segment its own definition of a win.

Take the three examples above. The suburban family segment probably converts best on Facebook and YouTube with school-district and neighborhood-tour content, and you might measure campaign success on booked showings per dollar. The young-professional rental segment leans on Instagram Reels and TikTok walkthroughs of the units and the neighborhood, with success measured by rental applications submitted. Retirees might respond better to a Google search or a referral-driven email, and success there could be measured by the number of in-person consultations booked.

2. Build a Consistent Brand Identity

Key Takeaways

  • Meta tags are HTML snippets in the <head> section of your page that tell search engines and AI tools what your content is about.

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. A social media target audience is the specific group of people most likely to engage with your brand on social, defined by demographics, interests, behaviors, and stage in the customer journey.
  2. Your social media audience is not the same as your target market. Most brands need several audience segments across different platforms and campaigns.
  3. Analytics, social listening, and competitor analysis are the most reliable ways to identify and refine who you are actually reaching.
  4. Reaching your audience means matching platform, format, and message to each segment, then testing and adjusting based on performance data.

What is a social media target audience?

A social media target audience is a specific group of people your brand wants to reach on social media, based on shared traits like interests, behaviors, and demographics.

These are the users most likely to engage with your content, respond to your messaging, and convert into customers.

It is worth separating this from your general marketing audience. Someone might be a perfect customer for your product and still never see a single post, because they do not use the platforms you publish on or engage with the formats you produce. Your social media audience is defined as much by platform behavior as by buying potential.

For example, Momofuku Goods shares recipes modified for home cooks on their Instagram account. Of course, they incorporate Momofuku Goods products, but the recipes address a core interest of its audience.

Source: Momofukugoods

Understanding their target audience’s interest in cooking is a major contributing factor explaining why the Goods brand itself has over 182,000 followers.

In short: Your social media target audience is the slice of people you can realistically reach, and reliably engage, on the platforms where you publish.

Download now!

Social media target audience vs. target market: What is the difference?

A target market is the broad group of potential customers for your product or service, while a social media target audience is the narrower subset you aim to reach with a specific campaign or on a specific platform.

The target market is a business decision. The target audience is a channel decision. A running shoe brand might define its target market as recreational runners aged 25 to 55 in North America. On TikTok, its target audience might be first-time marathon trainees aged 22 to 30 who follow race-day content. Same company, much tighter group.

The simplest way to hold the difference: Your target market tells you who to sell to, and your social media target audience tells you who to talk to today.

Why does defining your social media target audience matter?

Defining your audience matters because it determines where your budget goes, what you publish, and whether any of it produces results you can measure.

Broad targeting feels safe, but it usually means diluted messaging, wasted paid spend, and content that no single group finds particularly relevant. A clearly defined audience gives you:

  • Focused messaging: You write for a specific person instead of a hypothetical average, which makes content sharper and easier to produce at scale.
  • Better return on spend: Narrow ad targeting reduces wasted impressions and improves the efficiency of every campaign dollar. It also makes your social media ROI easier to attribute.
  • Smarter platform selection: Knowing where your audience already spends time keeps teams from maintaining channels that never deliver.
  • Stronger brand relationships: Relevance compounds. People who consistently see content that matches their interests are far more likely to stick around.

For larger teams, there is a governance benefit too. When audience definitions are documented and shared as part of your broader social strategy, regional teams and agencies stay consistent instead of interpreting the brand differently on every channel.

What are the types of social media target audiences?

Social media target audiences are usually grouped by one of five approaches: demographics, psychographics, behavioral signals, purchase intent, or existing customer status. Most brands use a combination rather than picking just one.

Here are the main types of audience segmentation to work with:

  • Demographics
  • Psychographics
  • Behavioral signals
  • Purchase intent
  • Existing customers

Demographics

Demographics cover age, gender, level of education, location, and income level. They are the easiest data to pull and the easiest place to start, since every native analytics tool reports them.

One caveat worth repeating: Your social media target audience may not share the same demographics as your target audience for other marketing efforts. The people who buy from you and the people who follow you are often two overlapping but distinct groups.

You spent time crafting what you thought was a great meta description for your page. You agonized over word choice and character count for what felt like hours, only to have Google ignore it and choose a random sentence from your content to display as the search snippet. 

Why?

The short answer is that Google rewrites roughly 70 percent of meta descriptions. A stat like that may have you wondering if it’s even worth writing them on your own.

It is. The 30 percent of descriptions that Google doesn’t rewrite are your best shot at controlling your first impression in search. My team and I have also discovered that the surviving descriptions share a few common traits.

This guide covers those traits, or meta description best practices. I’ll show you what can earn you clicks in 2026, backed by real examples from brands doing it well. By the end, you’ll have a framework you can take to your business immediately.

What Is a Meta Description?

A meta description is a short HTML tag that summarizes the page’s content.

This meta tag’s importance shows up in the snippet on the search engine results page, below the page URL and title.

The short answer is no. Meta descriptions aren’t a direct ranking factor, and Google has confirmed this explicitly through its search advocate, John Mueller, as well as its own search documentation.

articles.title: Social media image sizes for all networks [September 2026]
articles.fullContent:
Social media image sizes seem to change… a lot. And using the wrong dimensions can hurt reach, engagement, and brand consistency. 

This guide covers the current image size requirements for every major social platform in 2026.

Key takeaways

  1. Most social platforms still work best with images that are 1080 pixels wide, especially for feed and full-screen formats.
  2. Vertical, mobile-first aspect ratios like 4:5 and 9:16 now outperform square images on most networks.
  3. Tools like Perch by Hootsuite support network-specific resizing, making it easier for teams to stay consistent as specs change.

Quick social media image sizes

We go into more detail for every single network below, but this image includes the social media image sizes you probably look up most often.

Basic Instagram image sizes

  • Profile photo: 320 x 320 px
  • Landscape: 1080 x 566 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1350 px
  • Square: 1080 x 1080
  • Stories and Reels: 1080 x 1920

Basic Facebook image sizes

  • Profile photo: 196 x 196 px
  • Landscape: 1080 x 566 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1359 px
  • Square: 1080 x 1080 px
  • Stories and Reels: 1080 x 1920 px
  • Cover photo: 851 x 315 px

Basic X (formerly Twitter) image sizes

  • Profile photo: 400 x 400 px
  • Landscape: 1280 x 720 px
  • Vertical: 720 x 1280 px
  • Square: 720 x 720 px
  • Cover photo: 1500 x 500 px

Basic LinkedIn image sizes

  • Profile photo: 400 x 400 px
  • Landscape: 1200 x 627 px
  • Vertical: 720 x 900 px
  • Square: 1200 x 1200 px
  • Cover photo size: 1128 x 191 px

Basic TikTok image sizes

  • Profile photo: 20 x 20 px
  • Landscape (ad): 1920 x 1080 px
  • Vertical: 1080 x 1920 px
  • Square (ad): 640 x 640 px
  • Stories: 1080 x 1920 px

Instagram image sizes

Instagram supports horizontally and vertically oriented images well as square images. Well, sort of. You can still use all of these photo orientations in your posts, and that’s how they’ll appear in the Instagram feed. But they will all be displayed with a vertical crop on your Instagram grid.

This makes image dimensions a little tricky to get right, especially if you want to control the look of your grid as a cohesive whole. Follow these guidelines to make sure your images end up looking their best.

Instagram profile picture size: 320 x 320 pixels

Instagram profile photos are displayed at 110 x 100 pixels, but the image files are stored at 320 x 320 pixels, so make sure to upload an image that’s at least that big.

Even though the dimensions are in a square format, Instagram profile photos are displayed as a circle. Make sure any elements you want to focus on in the photo are centered so they don’t get cropped out.

Instagram post sizes:

  • Landscape image: 1080 x 566 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Vertical image: 1080 x 1350 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Square image: 1080 x 1080 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Carousel images: 1080 x 1350 pixels (feed) / 1012 x 1350 (grid)
  • Supported aspect ratios: Anywhere between 1.91:1 and 4:5 (feed) / 3:4 (grid)
  • Recommended image size: Width of 1080 pixels, height between 566 and 1350 pixels

Tips:

  • If you want your images to look their best on Instagram, aim to upload an image that is 1080 pixels wide.
  • When you share an Instagram image that’s sized over 1080 pixels, Instagram will size it down to 1080 pixels.
  • If you share a photo that has a resolution lower than 320 pixels, Instagram will size it up to 320 pixels.
  • If your image is between 320 and 1080 pixels wide, Instagram will keep that photo at its original resolution, “as long as the photo’s aspect ratio is between 1.91:1 and 4:5 (a height between 566 and 1350 pixels with a width of 1080 pixels).”
  • If you upload an image using a different ratio, the platform will automatically crop your photo to fit a supported ratio.
  • Remember that all photos appear in vertical format on your grid.

As social media users spread their attention across multiple platforms, more brands are expanding their presence to meet them there. According to our 2026 Social Media Content Strategy report, 87% of marketers plan to show up on more networks this year.

Cross-posting on social media is an excellent strategy for reaching new audiences, but it can also multiply your team’s workload, especially if you’re tailoring content to each platform.

This guide explains what cross-posting is, when it works (or backfires) and what each platform’s native rules allow. You’ll also learn how to cross-post easily with the Sprout Social Essentials plan.

What is cross-posting on social media?

Cross-posting means publishing the same content to two or more social media networks, either simultaneously or on a network-specific schedule.

But your posts shouldn’t be identical across platforms. A good cross-posting strategy preserves the core message or creative concept while optimizing the size, caption, format, tags, media and timing for each channel.

When you cross-post on social media effectively, you get content on your brand accounts quickly, freeing up your team for more strategic tasks like planning and engaging.

The right tools simplify the process. Sprout Social Essentials lets you cross-post to up to five social profiles at once. Use the unified Compose window to customize your post’s text, media and timing for each platform—no switching tabs.

Cross-posting vs. reposting vs. repurposing vs. sharing

Cross-posting, reposting, repurposing and sharing all extend the reach of your social content, but they describe different actions.

  • Cross-posting is when you publish your own content to several networks you control, with or without channel-specific editing.
  • Reposting is when you republish an existing post, yours or someone else’s, in its original form and usually within the same network.
  • Repurposing is when you rebuild an asset into one or several new formats to extend its life, increase reach and maximize ROI.
  • Sharing is when you distribute someone else’s post, either on your feed or to someone’s private inbox, through a native sharing button.

Here’s a quick table with examples of each term:

Term What it means Example Cross-posting Publishing one core post across multiple networks at the same time (or on an automated schedule) Publishing a ‘New Arrivals’ post on Instagram, LinkedIn and Facebook Reposting Resurfacing an existing post, yours or someone else’s, usually within the same network Reposting a customer’s Instagram post on your brand profile Repurposing Turning one asset into several different formats or deliverables Converting a webinar into three Reels and a LinkedIn carousel Sharing Distributing someone else’s post through a native sharing button Sharing a partner’s post to your feed or sending it through a direct message

Should you post the same content on every network?

Only cross-post content to networks where the topic is relevant and the format makes sense. Even then, “same content” should mean the same idea, not an untouched copy of the same post.

Exact duplication works for simple, time-sensitive updates. But for most campaigns, small changes to the hook, caption, tags, call-to-action, media and publish time give the post a better chance of meeting each audience’s expectations.

When cross-posting works well

Cross-posting works well when speed and consistency matter, or when audiences have similar needs across channels. Examples of content to cross-post include:

  • Company and product announcements: Launch dates, new locations, event registrations and important service updates benefit from a consistent message.
  • Evergreen education: Tips, how-to content, FAQs and research findings are useful across several networks, especially with minor tweaks.
  • Short-form video: A clean, watermark-free vertical video works across Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts.
  • Little to no audience overlap: If research shows your audience varies across platforms, cross-posting helps you reach more people without looking repetitive.

As for cadence, cross-post as often as the content fits each network, but balance it with platform-specific posts so every feed still feels original and worth following.

When to tailor or skip cross-posting

Create a separate post or stick to one network only when the content relies heavily on platform-specific behavior. Skip cross-posting in the following situations:

  • Format mismatch: A text-only update has no direct equivalent on TikTok, while a 10-minute landscape video won’t work on Instagram.
  • Overlapping audiences: Followers who see identical posts on several networks in quick succession will tune them out. Change the hook or stagger the timing.
  • Unique native features: Not every network supports features like polls, in-app sounds, stickers, live video, collaboration tools and document posts.
  • Varying audience expectations: Avoid cross-posting when content is built around platform-specific trends or needs a different angle, such as the business impact of an announcement on LinkedIn versus its human side on Instagram.

In these scenarios, the cons of cross-posting outweigh the pros. But that doesn’t mean cross-posting is bad for performance. Just avoid sharing identical or poorly adapted posts all the time as it makes your brand look repetitive and boring.

Benefits of cross-posting to multiple social channels

Cross-posting makes executing and scaling a multi-channel marketing strategy effortless. These five benefits show where cross-posting has the greatest impact.

Market to different target demographics

Cross-posting helps your brand reach different customer groups without recreating content from scratch every single time.

Every network has its own mix of age groups, interests, professions and behaviors. For example, the latest social media demographics show that Facebook reaches 88% of Baby Boomers, compared with 39% for Instagram and 20% for TikTok.

Key Takeaways

  • The best pay-per-click (PPC) agencies specialize in specific verticals. NP Digital leads in data-driven omnichannel campaigns, while many agencies focus on B2B, SaaS, or ecommerce.  
  • PPC agencies typically charge 10 to 20 percent of monthly ad spend, a flat retainer of $1,500 to $25,000 per month, or a hybrid of both. Setup fees run from $2,500 to $10,000.  
  • Google’s AI-powered tools like Smart Bidding and Performance Max are now baseline competencies for competitive PPC. Ask any agency you’re evaluating how they configure target return on ad spend (tROAS) and monitor AI-driven campaigns.  
  • Define your goals and success metrics before the discovery call. If you show up without clear key performance indicators, you’ll waste their time and money. You could even have less leverage at the negotiating table.  Check agencies against third-party review platforms like Clutch and G2. Then pressure-test their case studies against your own industry. 

Pay-per-click (PPC) advertising delivers an average return on investment (ROI) of 200 percent.  

Marketers are taking notice. About 93 percent of them view PPC advertising as effective or highly effective, second only to content marketing. 

A lot of that success depends on the PPC agency running your campaigns. Agencies aren’t interchangeable, though. The wrong partner can burn through your budget and compromise your results before you even launch. 

This article breaks down the best PPC agencies of 2026. Each one is highlighted for their expertise and specific strengths, helping you find the perfect partner who aligns with your goals and drives real results. 

Define Your Goals Before Hiring a PPC Agency

PPC campaigns can target drastically different outcomes, so you need to set clear goals and expectations before you start looking for an agency. Without them, you’ll have a hard time making an educated decision and could waste your time and money. 

Negotiating services with your agency of choice may also be a struggle without a clear target in mind. Scoping and pricing conversations generally fall to the agency if you don’t bring clear goals to the table, putting you in a weaker position at the signing table.  

So, before you get started, sit down with your team and decide what success looks like for your PPC campaigns.  

Your goals may include: 

  • Adding more qualified leads to your automated sales funnel 
  • Selling more of a specific product or category of products

Between all the DMs you need to answer and the posts you need to create, it’s time-consuming to maintain an active social media presence. And as you expand to more channels without increasing headcount, you get sucked into a productivity trap where you’re doing more work, but your results stagnate.

On the other hand, respondents who use dedicated tools to manage their social media are twice as likely to have enough time to get their work done.

This makes a strong case for marketers to start automating various aspects of their social media management. In this social media automation guide, we break down three essential steps to get started. Let’s take a look.

What social media automation means

Social media automation is the process of letting tools handle routine and repetitive tasks like scheduling posts or tracking brand mentions. This gives you back the time needed for more meaningful work that requires human input, whether that’s responding to your DMs or creating high-quality content.

Rather than “replacing you,” automation allows you to free up time by automating the routine. So you have more time to spend on personalizing the meaningful.

Step 1: Centralize your publishing

Connect your profiles to one dashboard

You waste time when you’re manually logging into different profiles to schedule every post individually. Streamline the process by connecting all your social media profiles to a centralized publishing dashboard.

A social media management platform like Sprout consolidates your publishing through a single dashboard. This lets you connect your profiles across different social networks and manage your publishing in one place. When you create a new post to schedule, all you have to do is select the profile(s) where you want to publish it.

Build a lightweight content calendar

Before all the automation comes the planning. And you need to plan your posts ahead of time before you can schedule them.

A content calendar makes it easy to do this and organize your publishing efforts. When you already have content planned for the entire week or month, you can quickly start creating posts without spending too much time on ideation.

And you don’t have to build an elaborate calendar, either. Keep it simple with a clear outline of the essentials:

  • Publishing date and time
  • Platform and profile
  • Content pillar or topic
  • Format

Sprout’s content calendar helps you visualize your planned posts across all your profiles. It lets you create and schedule posts directly within the calendar, which simplifies your publishing automation. You can even drag and drop posts to easily adjust your publishing cadence for optimal frequency.

Schedule around optimal send times

Effective publishing automation is highly strategic. It’s less about the publishing volume and more about the timing precision. When you schedule your posts to automatically go live, you need to time them to make sure they reach audiences when they’re most active.

Sprout’s social media automation features like Sprout Queue let you do just that. It automatically sends out your posts at a time of your choosing, so you no longer have to set reminders to remember when it’s time to post. You can schedule posts in bulk and for the entire month, freeing up time to focus on more high-impact tasks.

ViralPost™ takes the guesswork out of scheduling with optimal send time recommendations. It analyzes your audience and their engagement patterns to figure out when to deliver content for the greatest impact.

Many social media managers still handle engagement manually because they want to keep it human. But there are other aspects of engagement that you can automate without losing the human touch.

This starts with the process of tracking your comments, DMs and brand mentions. Automated Inbox Rules further help you manage your responses more efficiently by measuring and categorizing inbound messages. So it’s easy to see which messages you need to prioritize and which ones can wait for a bit.

Quick response times make brands stand out on social. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index™, nearly three-quarters of consumers expect a response within 24 hours. And 73% will even buy from a competitor if a brand doesn’t respond on social.

Reddit’s users lean young, making it a valuable social media platform for reaching Gen Z and younger millennials. While it reaches US audiences well, India, the United Kingdom and Canada also have notable bases.

articles.title: How to conduct a customer experience audit rooted in social intelligence
articles.fullContent:
Your customers are already telling you where their experience is falling short. The problem is, they don’t always tell you directly.

They post about it on social media, ask questions in comments, leave Google and Yelp reviews and talk about your brand in places your customer experience team may never see. Those conversations can expose frustrations, unmet needs and changing expectations that traditional feedback channels miss.

A customer experience audit gives you a structured way to evaluate those interactions across the customer journey. Building social intelligence into the process keeps the audit grounded in what customers are saying now and helps you decide what needs attention first.

In this article, we’ll break down what a customer experience audit involves, where social intelligence fits in and how to use the findings to improve the customer journey.

What is a customer experience audit?

A customer experience audit is a structured review of how people interact with your brand across the customer journey. It examines the touchpoints and feedback that shape the experience, from initial discovery through purchase and support.

Think of it like a health check for your customer experience. You’re looking at how different parts of the journey work together and where friction shows up between channels or departments.

A strong CX audit also looks beyond the channels your business owns. Social conversations and customer care interactions add context that surveys or CRM data alone may not capture, giving you a stronger foundation for what to improve.

5 steps for a modern customer experience audit that drives action

A customer experience audit works best when you approach it systematically. Here’s how to move from deciding what you want to learn to tracking whether your changes are working.

1. Set expectations for your CX audit

Before you pull data or review touchpoints, set the audit parameters. The steps below will help you establish what you’re trying to accomplish and what it will take to get there.

Involve the right stakeholders

Customer experience rarely sits with one department. Bring in people who own different parts of the journey, such as customer care, CX, social, marketing, PR and data analysts. Each group may catch gaps others miss.

Clarify everyone’s role upfront, too. Decide who will lead the audit, who will provide data or context and who needs to act on the findings.

Determine objectives and goals

Next, decide what you want to learn or improve. You might be trying to understand why customers abandon checkout after clicking through from social, improve response times on social or figure out where the brand experience feels inconsistent across channels.

Tie those objectives to specific parts of the customer journey and the outcomes that matter most. This will guide which touchpoints and metrics you review later.

Define scope

A CX audit can expand quickly across channels, customer groups and stages of the journey, so set boundaries before you begin.

Based on your objectives, decide what needs attention now based on your specific business priorities. That might mean auditing one priority audience across the full lifecycle or zeroing in on a stage where you already know there’s friction. Future audits can broaden the scope as new questions arise.

2. Map the customer journey across touch points

Customer journeys rarely follow a neat, predictable path. People move between channels and platforms as they discover brands, weigh their options and get support, making it harder to see the full experience in one place.

Mapping those touchpoints reveals how the pieces connect and where social media plays a role.

Capture the full customer lifecycle from discovery through care

Social influences customers at several key points in their relationship with your brand:

  • Product discovery: According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, around a third of consumers prefer social search for product reviews.
  • Purchase: Sprout’s State of Influencer Marketing Report found that 86% of consumers make an influencer-inspired purchase at least once a year.
  • Customer care: The Sprout Social Index™ found that 73% of social media users expect brands to respond on social within 24 hours.

Mapping your social media marketing funnel alongside the broader customer journey helps account for those interactions from discovery through ongoing social customer care.

Look beyond owned channels

Build your audit from the places customers interact with or talk about your brand. Alongside your own social posts and ads, include replies, DMs, chatbot interactions, reviews, customer posts, social shopping activity and traffic from social to your website. Widen the lens to review sites, discussion forums, influencer communities, media coverage and mentions that may never reach your profiles.

Sprout helps bring more of those touchpoints into one workflow. The Smart Inbox centralizes incoming social messages, while Reviews pulls customer feedback from sources including Google Business Profile, Yelp, Trustpilot and TripAdvisor. Sprout Social Listening bridges direct and indirect interactions, surfacing conversations about your brand and market that may not tag or mention you directly. Together, these tools give you a broader pool of customer conversations to draw from during the audit.

Connect social with the systems other teams use, too. The Sprout Social Salesforce integration enriches CRM profiles with social data, while Sprout’s Tableau BI Connector combines social with other business data for a fuller view of the journey.

3. Use social intelligence to identify pain points and gaps in customer experience

With the customer journey mapped, it’s time to diagnose what’s happening within it. Where is frustration building? What questions keep coming up? Are expectations changing faster than your experience can keep pace with?

Social intelligence helps answer those questions by illustrating how customer sentiment and conversation patterns are changing across the market.

Analyze audience sentiment

Look at how customers feel at key points in the journey. A drop in sentiment around a product launch or an increase in negative customer care messages can point to experiences worth investigating.

Social listening helps track sentiment across broader conversations, while Sprout’s Sentiment for Messages classifies incoming messages and reviews, enabling teams to identify interactions that need attention. NewsWhip by Sprout Social further adds predictive media intelligence to indicate when stories or issues are gaining traction.

You know the question: How did the campaign perform? 

Giving a useful answer can mean moving between numerous dashboards and spreadsheets.  The summary may take only a few minutes to read, but it took you hours to assemble.

Instead, try asking Trellis:

Back comes three creative drivers with the posts that prove each one, written with an executive audience in mind. You bring the context and judgement; Trellis gives you a better starting point.

Snapchat publishing:  Snapchat reports more than 971 million monthly active users globally, and reaching them now takes the same workflow as every other network you run. Connect a Public Profile and you compose and tailor Spotlights and Stories in the same window as everything else.

Spend less time moving between Sprout and Instagram

Instagram picked up several updates in August, each designed to keep more of the everyday work inside your existing Sprout workflow.
